front_blocks.md: Define **covalent bond**.

back_blocks.md: A **covalent bond** is a bond formed between atoms by the sharing of a pair of **electrons**.

cards.front_md: Define **covalent bond**.
cards.back_md: A **covalent bond** is a bond formed between atoms by the sharing of a pair of **electrons**.

front_blocks.md: In a covalent bond, each atom usually provides **..........** of the electrons in the shared pair.

back_blocks.md: In a covalent bond, each atom usually provides **one** of the electrons in the shared pair.

cards.front_md: In a covalent bond, each atom usually provides **..........** of the electrons in the shared pair.
cards.back_md: In a covalent bond, each atom usually provides **one** of the electrons in the shared pair.

front_blocks.md: **True or False?**
Covalent bonds form between non-metal atoms only.

back_blocks.md: **True.**
Covalent bonds form when non-metal atoms share pairs of electrons to achieve a full outer shell.

cards.front_md:
**True or False?**

Covalent bonds form between non-metal atoms only.
cards.back_md:
**True.**

Covalent bonds form when non-metal atoms share pairs of electrons to achieve a full outer shell.

front_blocks.md: Why do non-metal atoms form covalent bonds?

back_blocks.md: Non-metal atoms form covalent bonds to achieve a full outer shell of electrons, which gives each atom a more stable electron configuration similar to a noble gas.

cards.front_md: Why do non-metal atoms form covalent bonds?
cards.back_md: Non-metal atoms form covalent bonds to achieve a full outer shell of electrons, which gives each atom a more stable electron configuration similar to a noble gas.

front_blocks.md: Define **bonding electrons**.

back_blocks.md: **Bonding electrons** are shared electrons that form a **covalent bond**, always occurring in pairs.

cards.front_md: Define **bonding electrons**.
cards.back_md: **Bonding electrons** are shared electrons that form a **covalent bond**, always occurring in pairs.

front_blocks.md: Electrons in the outer shell that are **not** involved in a covalent bond are called **..........** electrons.

back_blocks.md: Electrons in the outer shell that are **not** involved in a covalent bond are called **non-bonding** electrons.

cards.front_md: Electrons in the outer shell that are **not** involved in a covalent bond are called **..........** electrons.
cards.back_md: Electrons in the outer shell that are **not** involved in a covalent bond are called **non-bonding** electrons.

front_blocks.md: **True or False?**
In a covalent bond, electrons are transferred from one atom to the other.

back_blocks.md: **False.**
In a covalent bond electrons are **shared** between atoms, not transferred. Electron transfer occurs in ionic bonding.

cards.front_md:
**True or False?**

In a covalent bond, electrons are transferred from one atom to the other.
cards.back_md:
**False.**

In a covalent bond electrons are **shared** between atoms, not transferred. Electron transfer occurs in ionic bonding.

front_blocks.md: What holds the atoms together in a covalent bond?

back_blocks.md: The atoms are held together by the strong **electrostatic attraction** between the positively charged nuclei of both atoms and the negatively charged shared pair of electrons.

cards.front_md: What holds the atoms together in a covalent bond?
cards.back_md: The atoms are held together by the strong **electrostatic attraction** between the positively charged nuclei of both atoms and the negatively charged shared pair of electrons.

front_blocks.md: Define **non-bonding electrons**.

back_blocks.md: **Non-bonding electrons** are outer-shell electrons that are not involved in any **covalent bond** and do not form part of a shared pair.

cards.front_md: Define **non-bonding electrons**.

front_blocks.md: **True or False?**
Covalent bonds are weak and easily broken at room temperature.

back_blocks.md: **False.**
Covalent bonds between atoms are very **strong** and require significant energy to break.

cards.front_md:
**True or False?**

front_blocks.md: Define **dot and cross diagram**.

back_blocks.md: A **dot and cross diagram** is a representation of a molecule that shows the arrangement and sharing of outer-shell electrons between bonded atoms.

cards.front_md: Define **dot and cross diagram**.
cards.back_md: A **dot and cross diagram** is a representation of a molecule that shows the arrangement and sharing of outer-shell electrons between bonded atoms.

front_blocks.md: What does each covalent bond represent in a dot and cross diagram?

back_blocks.md: Each covalent bond represents one **shared pair of electrons**, with one electron contributed by each of the two bonded atoms.

cards.front_md: What does each covalent bond represent in a dot and cross diagram?
cards.back_md: Each covalent bond represents one **shared pair of electrons**, with one electron contributed by each of the two bonded atoms.

front_blocks.md: In a dot and cross diagram, dots and crosses are used to show electrons from **..........** different atoms so their origins can be distinguished.

back_blocks.md: In a dot and cross diagram, dots and crosses are used to show electrons from **two** different atoms so their origins can be distinguished.

front_blocks.md: **True or False?**
A nitrogen molecule, N<sub>2</sub>, contains a triple covalent bond.

back_blocks.md: **True.**
Each nitrogen atom has five outer electrons and needs three more to fill its shell, so the two nitrogen atoms share **three pairs** of electrons forming a **triple bond**.

front_blocks.md: How many covalent bonds does each carbon atom form in methane, CH<sub>4</sub>?

back_blocks.md: Each carbon atom forms **four** covalent bonds in methane, one with each hydrogen atom, giving carbon a full outer shell of eight electrons.

front_blocks.md: **True or False?**
In ammonia, NH<sub>3</sub>, the nitrogen atom has one non-bonding pair of electrons.

back_blocks.md: **True.**
Nitrogen forms three covalent bonds with the three hydrogen atoms, leaving one **non-bonding pair** of outer-shell electrons.

front_blocks.md: How many shared pairs of electrons are shown in the dot and cross diagram for CO<sub>2</sub>?

back_blocks.md: The dot and cross diagram for CO<sub>2</sub> shows **four** shared pairs of electrons in total: two shared pairs (a double bond) between carbon and each oxygen atom.

front_blocks.md: Define **simple molecule**.

back_blocks.md: A **simple molecule** is a small covalently bonded molecule consisting of a fixed small number of atoms joined by shared electron pairs.

cards.front_md: Define **simple molecule**.

front_blocks.md: In a dot and cross diagram for H<sub>2</sub>O, how many non-bonding pairs of electrons does the oxygen atom have?

back_blocks.md: The oxygen atom in H<sub>2</sub>O has **two** non-bonding pairs of electrons: oxygen forms two covalent bonds with the hydrogen atoms, leaving two pairs unused.

cards.front_md: In a dot and cross diagram for H<sub>2</sub>O, how many non-bonding pairs of electrons does the oxygen atom have?

front_blocks.md: Define **simple molecular structure**.

back_blocks.md: A **simple molecular structure** is one in which small covalently bonded molecules are held together by weak **intermolecular forces**, giving low melting and boiling points.

cards.front_md: Define **simple molecular structure**.
cards.back_md: A **simple molecular structure** is one in which small covalently bonded molecules are held together by weak **intermolecular forces**, giving low melting and boiling points.

front_blocks.md: Why do simple molecular structures have low melting and boiling points?

back_blocks.md: Simple molecular structures have low melting and boiling points because the **intermolecular forces** between molecules are weak and require little energy to overcome.

cards.front_md: Why do simple molecular structures have low melting and boiling points?
cards.back_md: Simple molecular structures have low melting and boiling points because the **intermolecular forces** between molecules are weak and require little energy to overcome.

front_blocks.md: **True or False?**
When a simple molecular substance melts, its covalent bonds are broken.

back_blocks.md: **False.**
When a simple molecular substance melts it is the weak **intermolecular forces** between molecules that are overcome, not the strong **covalent bonds** within the molecules.

cards.front_md:
**True or False?**

When a simple molecular substance melts, its covalent bonds are broken.

**False.**

back_blocks.md: Simple molecular structures generally **do not** conduct electricity because they have no free **ions** or electrons.

front_blocks.md: How does increasing relative molecular mass affect the melting point of a simple molecular substance?

back_blocks.md: As **relative molecular mass** increases, the melting point generally increases because larger molecules have stronger intermolecular forces that require more energy to overcome.

front_blocks.md: Define **intermolecular forces**.

back_blocks.md: **Intermolecular forces** are weak forces of attraction that act between neighbouring molecules in a simple molecular substance.

front_blocks.md: **True or False?**
C<sub>60</sub> fullerene can conduct electricity because it contains delocalised electrons.

back_blocks.md: **False.**

C<sub>60</sub> fullerene has a **simple molecular structure**. Although electrons exist within each molecule, they **cannot move between the separate molecules**, so C<sub>60</sub> **cannot conduct electricity**.

back_blocks.md: Buckminsterfullerene consists of **60** carbon atoms arranged in hexagons and pentagons to form a hollow **sphere** shape.

front_blocks.md: Why are fullerenes useful for drug delivery?

back_blocks.md: Fullerenes can trap other molecules inside their hollow **sphere** or tube structure, allowing them to carry and deliver drug molecules to specific targets in the body.

Most simple molecular substances are gases or liquids at room temperature.

back_blocks.md: **True.**
The weak **intermolecular forces** between simple molecules require little energy to overcome, so most exist as gases or liquids under normal conditions.

front_blocks.md: Define **giant covalent structure**.

back_blocks.md: A **giant covalent structure** is a lattice of a very large number of non-metal atoms all joined by strong **covalent bonds** throughout the structure.

front_blocks.md: Why do giant covalent structures have very high melting points?

back_blocks.md: Giant covalent structures have very high melting points because they contain many strong **covalent bonds** throughout the lattice that require a large amount of energy to break.

Diamond can conduct electricity.

back_blocks.md: **False.**
Diamond cannot conduct electricity because all four outer electrons of each carbon atom are used in **covalent bonds**, leaving no free or **delocalised electrons** to carry charge.

front_blocks.md: Why is diamond extremely hard?

back_blocks.md: Diamond is extremely **hard** because each carbon atom is bonded to four others by strong covalent bonds in all directions, making the structure rigid and resistant to scratching.

front_blocks.md: Define **allotropes**.

back_blocks.md: **Allotropes** are different structural forms of the same element in the same physical state, such as **diamond** and **graphite** which are both forms of carbon.

back_blocks.md: In graphite, each carbon atom bonds to **three** others, forming layers of hexagons with one **delocalised** electron per carbon atom.

Graphite can conduct electricity because it has delocalised electrons.

back_blocks.md: **True.**
Each carbon atom in graphite forms only three bonds, leaving one electron per atom **delocalised** and free to move through the layers and carry charge.

front_blocks.md: Why is graphite soft and slippery?

back_blocks.md: Graphite is soft and slippery because its carbon atoms are arranged in layers held together by only **weak forces**, allowing the layers to slide over each other easily.

Diamond and graphite have different melting points because one is a giant covalent structure and the other is not.

back_blocks.md: **False.**
Both diamond and graphite are **giant covalent structures** with high melting points. Their other properties differ because of the different bonding arrangements within each structure.
